result.compliance_and_security:
ToU DE LA STEAM WEB API (2010)
- La clave solo existe en GitHub Secrets (pipeline) y como secret del Worker (M5).
  · Viaja en la cabecera x-webapi-key, nunca en la query, para que no acabe en logs.
  · Nunca va en el instalador, el binario ni el webview. El CI escanea el .exe y el instalador buscando el patrón de la clave.
  · Solo se usa api.steampowered.com, nunca partner.steam-api.com.
- Uso muy por debajo de las 100.000 llamadas/día, con limitador propio en cada salida.
- Los datos de un usuario se piden solo cuando él lo solicita (importar o comprobar). Por defecto no hay sondeos en segundo plano.
- Política de privacidad (obligatoria): explica qué datos de Steam se guardan (steamID64, y la wishlist, los juegos, el tiempo jugado y los logros importados) y en qué países. Se guardan en el dispositivo y, si se activa la sync, en Cloudflare D1 (con ubicación o jurisdicción UE si está disponible). El origen es Valve, en EE. UU.
- Sin dar a entender que Valve respalda la app:
  · «Steam» no aparece en el nombre ni en el icono, y solo se usa para describir («Importar desde Steam»).
  · Aviso de marcas en Acerca de: «GameAgenda no está afiliado a Valve; Steam es una marca de Valve Corporation».
  · Se usan las imágenes oficiales del botón «Sign in through Steam».
- Nunca se piden contraseñas ni tokens de Steam, nunca se usa PICS. PlayStation solo se marca a mano, sin NPSSO.

RGPD / LOPDGDD (ESPAÑA)
- M1-M3: los datos de la agenda no salen del dispositivo. Solo tratamos la IP en el CDN; además, la IP llega a Steam en las llamadas directas.
- Las portadas se cargan del CDN de Steam, así que la IP del usuario llega a Valve/Akamai. Se avisa en la primera capa y hay un ajuste «No cargar portadas».
- M4-M5:
  · Base jurídica: art. 6.1.b (prestar el servicio que pide el usuario).
  · Minimización: sin email ni nombre, espacio seudónimo, y el steamID64 no se sincroniza.
  · Derechos: exportar (JSON) y borrar (en local, y con DELETE del espacio en el servidor).
  · Información por capas: la primera al activar la sync o Steam; la segunda, una página completa.
  · Registro de actividades con Facilita RGPD de la AEPD. Encargados: Cloudflare (con DPA) y GitHub (CI, sin datos personales).
  · Edad mínima de 14 años para las funciones online (16 si cambia la ley), con una casilla de declaración.
- Solo se usa almacenamiento estrictamente necesario, así que no hace falta banner. No hay analítica; si se añade, será con consentimiento previo.
- El portapapeles solo se lee al abrir Quick-add, solo para detectar enlaces, y no se guarda.

SEGURIDAD TÉCNICA
- Capabilities mínimas en Tauri: el webview solo tiene core:default y los comandos propios, sin http:, fs: ni shell:. Las URLs y los diálogos se abren desde Rust con una lista blanca: store.steampowered.com, steamcommunity.com y nuestra web.
- CSP: default-src 'self' ipc: http://ipc.localhost; img-src 'self' data: https://shared.akamai.steamstatic.com; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'. No se carga código remoto.
- SQL siempre con parámetros; el MATCH se construye con tokens entrecomillados y escapados.
- Límites de entrada: título de 300 caracteres como máximo, nota de 10.000, nombre de flag de 40 y appid entre 1 y 2^24-1.
- Las respuestas de Steam y del CDN se tratan como datos no fiables: tamaño máximo (8 MiB para la API, 64 MiB para el snapshot), timeouts, deserialización tipada con serde y sha256 comprobado contra el manifest. La firma ed25519 del manifest queda en el backlog.
- Los deep links solo aceptan una lista blanca de acciones (add y steam/linked) y nunca borran nada. El traspaso de Steam es al estilo PKCE.
- El updater se firma con minisign, con la clave privada fuera del repo.
- cargo audit (cargo install cargo-audit) y npm audit en el CI; lockfiles en el repo.

FUENTES FUTURAS
- IGDB para PlayStation y otras plataformas:
  · gratis, incluso para uso comercial, con su programa de partners y atribución visible;
  · solo desde el backend, a 4 req/s y 8 peticiones simultáneas;
  · external_games con source 1 = appid de Steam.
- PSN: platinado manual (las APIs NPSSO no oficiales suponen riesgo de ToS).
- ITAD para precios, preguntando antes (sus términos prohíben apps competidoras).
- Evitar: scraping de HLTB, Giant Bomb, copiar en masa RAWG, automatizar SteamGridDB y los datos de PCGamingWiki (licencia no comercial).
result.performance_plan:
PRESUPUESTOS: CÓMO SE CUMPLEN Y CÓMO SE MIDEN

1) De la tecla a los resultados: 50 ms o menos en p95
Cómo se cumple:
- Búsqueda local, sin red ni debounce.
- FTS5 trigram mide 0,14-0,45 ms. A eso se suman, estimados: carga de candidatos y ranking (<1 ms), IPC (1-3 ms) y render de 30 filas como máximo (3-8 ms).
- Las miniaturas se cargan en diferido con tamaño fijo, así que no bloquean el render.
- Las respuestas obsoletas se descartan por número de secuencia.
- Conexión de lectura dedicada, con prepare_cached y cache_size de 32 MiB.
- Compilación con opt-level 3, y dependencias optimizadas también en dev.
Cómo se mide:
- search_bench en Rust con 2.000 consultas: prefijos de los 1.000 títulos más populares, 300 consultas reales en español y 50 con erratas. Da p50/p95/p99; el objetivo es un p95 de 2 ms o menos.
- Playwright por CDP escribe 200 consultas carácter a carácter. La UI marca performance.mark en el keydown y mide al terminar el commit (rAF tras useLayoutEffect). Objetivo: p95 de 50 ms o menos, también mientras se aplica un delta en segundo plano.

2) Del toque a la respuesta visual: 100 ms o menos
Cómo se cumple: UI optimista (el estado cambia en el mismo frame), la escritura en SQLite tarda milisegundos en otro hilo, y si falla se revierte con un aviso.
Cómo se mide: Event Timing API (PerformanceObserver de tipo 'event', durationThreshold 16) en las builds de dev/E2E. Objetivo: p95 de 100 ms o menos.

3) INP: p75 de 200 ms o menos
Cómo se mide: web-vitals 6.2.3 (onINP) durante una sesión E2E de 5 min con guion: Agenda, Explorar con scroll largo y Quick-add. En escritorio se espera muy por debajo de 100 ms.
Cómo se cumple en Explorar: virtualización, páginas de 200 filas y precarga.

4) Primera visita (LCP de 2,5 s o menos)
- Escritorio, su equivalente: del primer arranque a poder buscar en 3 s o menos. El seed va dentro de la app (no hace falta red) y el escaneo bruto cubre la búsqueda mientras el FTS se construye en segundo plano, con progreso por Channel. Se mide con %LOCALAPPDATA% limpio.
- PWA (M4): la shell ocupa 150 KB gzip como máximo. El catálogo (.tsv.gz) llega después del primer pintado y el índice se construye en un Worker. Objetivo: LCP de 2,5 s o menos en Lighthouse móvil (4G lenta).

5) Reinicio con caché: 2 s o menos
Cómo se cumple:
- La ventana sigue oculta hasta el primer pintado (app_ready → show()), sin destello blanco.
- Las bases de datos se abren mientras se crea el WebView2.
- No se construye ningún índice al arrancar (el FTS se guarda en disco).
- La comprobación del manifest se retrasa 10 s.
Cómo se mide: marcas de tiempo en main() (Instant), en RunEvent::Ready y en el primer pintado de JS, y startup_ms al log. Un script arranca la app 10 veces; objetivo p95 de 2 s o menos, con 1,5 s como meta.
- PWA: service worker cache-first y datos en IndexedDB; la agenda se muestra antes de que el índice esté listo.

MÓVILES (PWA)
Los móviles son varias veces más lentos (sin medir todavía), así que se usa el índice de prefijos por palabra: 0-0,3 ms por consulta, 220-330 ms de construcción y ~16 MiB en este PC. La fuerza bruta (7-14 ms aquí) quedaría demasiado cerca de 50 ms en un móvil. Se mide:
- en un Android de gama media, con la depuración remota de Chrome;
- en un iPhone, con un overlay de tiempos en pantalla, porque sin Mac no hay Web Inspector de Safari.

REGRESIONES
El bench de Rust y el E2E de rendimiento se ejecutan antes de cada release (npm run perf). En el CI van con un umbral más holgado, porque los runners compartidos dan medidas ruidosas.

milestones.name: M1 · Catálogo completo de Steam + búsqueda + añadir rápido (escritorio)
milestones.scope: Monorepo (npm workspaces + Cargo workspace) con CI de lint, typecheck y tests. Pipeline v1: GetAppList con clave (4 llamadas) + Query semanal (~197) + GetItems para huecos → games-<ver>.tsv.br/.gz + manifest con gates de validación → Cloudflare static assets; cron diario y semanal con aviso de inactividad. Hasta tener la clave, se usa el fixture jsnli/steamappidlist solo en dev. Escritorio con Tauri 2.12.5: ga-core con catalog.db (seed incluido en el instalador + descarga del último snapshot), FTS5 trigram, prefijos, reordenación y escaneo bruto en el primer arranque. Explorar: lista virtualizada de todos los juegos, con orden y filtros y los adultos ocultos. Quick-add con atajo global y bandeja: Enter añade a «Quiero jugar», un juego manual se crea con solo el título, y se puede pegar un enlace o un appid. Vista Quiero jugar con quitar y deshacer.
milestones.acceptance: (1) Explorar muestra el recuento del manifest (~196,6k) y se puede recorrer de la primera a la última fila; Lanzados + Próximamente suman Todos. (2) Con 2.000 filas al azar, el nombre exacto pone su appid en el top 5 en al menos el 99% de los casos; con los 1.000 más populares, 4 letras de la palabra principal lo ponen en el top 10 en al menos el 90%. (3) De la tecla al pintado, p95 de 50 ms o menos (Playwright por CDP, build release, 200 consultas), y search_bench con p95 de 2 ms o menos. (4) Atajo, escribir y Enter en 3 s o menos en 10 de 10 intentos (mediana de 2 s o menos); del toque a la respuesta visual, p95 de 100 ms o menos. (5) 20 enlaces de prueba dan el appid correcto, y un appid desconocido se añade como provisional. (6) En el primer arranque sin red se puede buscar en 3 s o menos gracias al seed; el reinicio con caché tiene un p95 de 2 s o menos. (7) El escaneo de cadenas del instalador no encuentra la clave.

milestones.name: M2 · Agenda completa: estados, flags, notas y portadas
milestones.scope: 5 estados; Platinado ⇒ Completado, Comprado y Próximo, más flags personalizados; nota; fechas que se rellenan solas; filtros, orden y contadores; teclas 1-5, P, C, N y Supr con deshacer en todo. Cliente Steam nativo: cola de 1 req/s como máximo, backoff y pausa global ante un 429. GetItems bajo demanda (library_capsule → header → placeholder, sin adivinar nombres de fichero) con caché de 30 días; nombre ES, fecha y resumen de reseñas en la ficha. Exportar e importar JSON, backups diarios con VACUUM INTO y ajustes (atajo, país, adultos, portadas sí/no).
milestones.acceptance: (1) Tests de transiciones: Platinado pasa a Completado y rellena completed_at, y deshacer deja exactamente el estado anterior. (2) Una agenda de 300 juegos pinta sus portadas desde caché en 1 s o menos, y en frío hace 2 llamadas a GetItems como máximo. (3) Con GetItems bloqueado (429/404 simulados) se ven placeholders, no salta ningún error modal y la cola se pausa. (4) Exportar, borrar e importar deja las filas idénticas. (5) Los backups rotan y se guardan los 7 últimos.

milestones.name: M3 · Catálogo siempre al día + captura avanzada en escritorio
milestones.scope: Pipeline: el lane diario hace el diff (altas, cambios, y bajas clasificadas como retirado o inexistente con GetItems), con una cadena de 14 deltas y flags de cliente en el manifest. Cliente: aplica los deltas o el snapshot completo con sha256, sin bloquear la búsqueda. Calidad de búsqueda: fuzzy de trigramas, alias en CSV, números romanos, artículos iniciales y un conjunto de 300 consultas reales en español. Deep link gameagenda://add, bookmarklet y arrastrar enlaces; arranque opcional en la bandeja al iniciar Windows; updater firmado (releases construidas en local, latest.json en Cloudflare).
milestones.acceptance: (1) Un delta de 3,3k filas se aplica en 500 ms o menos, en segundo plano, sin que la búsqueda se pare más de 50 ms. (2) Un juego retirado desaparece de la búsqueda pero sigue en la agenda con su título. (3) Top 5 en al menos el 85% de las 300 consultas, incluidas 30 con erratas. (4) Desde una página de la tienda, el bookmarklet añade el juego en 2 s o menos. (5) La actualización de 0.1.0 a 0.1.1 se instala tras verificar la firma.

milestones.name: M4 · Captura en el móvil: PWA compañera + relay de sync
milestones.scope: Worker con Hono 4.13.14 + D1: espacios seudónimos, push, pull, borrado e inbox; emparejamiento por QR; cliente de sync en ga-core (outbox, HLC, LWW). PWA con Vite 8.3.5 + React 19.3.1 + vite-plugin-pwa 2.0.0 + Dexie 4.4.7: instalable y offline, con el snapshot .tsv.gz y un índice de prefijos en un Web Worker. Incluye alta rápida (catálogo, enlace o manual), agenda con estados y flags, Web Share Target, storage.persist() y exportación.
milestones.acceptance: (1) Con la PWA instalada, apuntar un juego en el móvil lleva 3 s o menos. (2) Lo apuntado en el móvil llega al escritorio en cuanto se enfoca su ventana, o en 60 s como máximo si ya está enfocada. (3) Un test automatizado con dos dispositivos editando la misma entrada sin conexión acaba convergiendo (LWW). (4) La PWA da un LCP de 2,5 s o menos en Lighthouse móvil y reinicia con caché en 2 s o menos. (5) El Worker gasta menos de 10 ms de CPU por petición. (6) Hacer DELETE del espacio no deja ninguna fila.

milestones.name: M5 · Cuenta de Steam (opcional): wishlist, comprados y logros
milestones.scope: Pegar el perfil → steamID64 (?xml=1) → importar la wishlist sin clave a Quiero jugar. «Iniciar sesión a través de Steam» → Worker (OpenID + check_authentication con steam-signin 1.0.5) → GetOwnedGames con la clave → entrega de un solo uso al estilo PKCE → marcar Comprado (sin lo compartido en familia) y backlog opcional. Comprobación de logros por juego para sugerir Platinado. Pantalla «Datos de Steam que guardamos», aviso de marcas, botón oficial, información de privacidad por capas y botón para borrar los datos de Steam.
milestones.acceptance: (1) Una biblioteca de 1.000 juegos se importa de principio a fin en 30 s o menos. (2) Con un perfil privado aparece un mensaje que explica qué cambiar. (3) Tras el traspaso, D1 no guarda ningún dato de Steam. (4) El escaneo del binario no encuentra la clave. (5) Un solo botón borra todo lo que viene de Steam.

milestones.name: M6 · Tauri Android (opcional, después del prototipo)
milestones.scope: Instalar Android Studio, el SDK/NDK y su JBR; tauri android init; compilar ga-core (rusqlite bundled) para Android; adaptar las pantallas al tacto; un plugin Kotlin para recibir ACTION_SEND (compartir un enlace) que reutiliza la lógica de enlaces. La sync es la misma de M4.
milestones.acceptance: (1) La APK de depuración funciona en un Android real. (2) Compartir un enlace de Steam añade el juego en 3 s o menos. (3) La búsqueda tiene un p95 de 50 ms o menos en el dispositivo. (4) Sincroniza con el escritorio.

risks.risk: Los endpoints sin clave (IStoreQueryService/Query e IStoreBrowseService/GetItems) no están documentados y pueden cambiar o desaparecer sin aviso.
risks.mitigation: Los nombres y appids salen de GetAppList, que sí está documentado. Cada dato de enriquecimiento es opcional y tiene un plan B: sin popularidad, se ordena por tipo de coincidencia y longitud del título; sin portadas, placeholders. El pipeline valida el esquema, y el flag remoto store_browse del manifest apaga las llamadas de los clientes. Si Query falla, se hace un pase completo con GetItems (~983 llamadas, unos 41 min a la semana).

risks.risk: Los límites de peticiones no están documentados: las IPs compartidas de los runners de GitHub o un uso intenso del cliente pueden provocar errores 429 o bloqueos.
risks.mitigation: Un solo worker en cada sitio: 0,4 req/s como máximo sostenido en el pipeline y ráfagas de 1 req/s como máximo en el cliente, con backoff exponencial y pausa global. El pipeline guarda puntos de control para reanudar y, como plan B, se ejecuta en este PC con el Programador de tareas. El cliente solo llama cuando lo necesita y cachea 30 días.

risks.risk: El cron de GitHub Actions puede llegar tarde, perderse o desactivarse tras 60 días sin actividad.
risks.mitigation: El cliente funciona con cualquier versión del catálogo, y pegar un enlace o appid resuelve las novedades. Un aviso de inactividad manda un email; el pipeline se puede lanzar a mano (workflow_dispatch) o en local, y la app muestra la edad del catálogo.

risks.risk: La clave de Steam exige una cuenta no limitada (5 US$ gastados como mínimo) y Steam Guard móvil, y además puede revocarse.
risks.mitigation: Pedirla el primer día y, mientras tanto, usar el fixture jsnli/steamappidlist solo en desarrollo. Si se revoca, los clientes conservan el último catálogo y Query sin clave (~197 llamadas) sirve de lista temporal.

risks.risk: Lo habitual es apuntar juegos desde el móvil, y este enfoque no llega ahí hasta M4; iOS nunca tendrá app nativa ni Share Target.
risks.mitigation: Se deja claro desde el principio. M4 puede adelantarse a justo después de M1 si las pruebas con usuarios lo piden, porque la PWA reutiliza packages/core y el mismo snapshot. En Android hay Share Target; en iOS, pegar el enlace o un Atajo de iOS.

risks.risk: Rust tiene curva de aprendizaje y compila despacio para un desarrollador en solitario.
risks.mitigation: ga-core es pequeño y está aislado (~1,5k líneas: base de datos, búsqueda, importación y cliente Steam). Las dependencias se compilan optimizadas también en dev, la compilación es incremental y la UI en TS se recarga en caliente. Se evitan las macros y los genéricos complicados.

risks.risk: Sin firmar el instalador, Windows SmartScreen muestra avisos, y Azure Artifact Signing no parece estar disponible para particulares en la UE.
risks.mitigation: Instrucciones claras para los pocos testers del prototipo. Antes de una beta pública, valorar un certificado OV, la Microsoft Store o firmar a través de una empresa.

risks.risk: Tauri 3 está en alpha (3.0.0-alpha.5): los plugins cambian y la documentación de las dos versiones se mezcla.
risks.mitigation: Dependencias con caret 2.x y lockfiles en el repo. No se actualiza durante el prototipo; la migración se hace con la guía oficial cuando 3.x sea estable.

risks.risk: Hay lógica duplicada entre Rust (escritorio) y TS (PWA): fold, enlaces y reglas de estado.
risks.mitigation: Los mismos vectores de prueba JSON se ejecutan en cargo test y en Vitest. Si la duplicación crece, esa lógica pura se compila a WASM.

risks.risk: Pérdida de datos: todo es local y no hay sync hasta M4.
risks.mitigation: user.db con synchronous=FULL, copia diaria rotativa con VACUUM INTO, copia opcional a OneDrive y exportación JSON.

risks.risk: Calidad de búsqueda: siglas, erratas, nombres traducidos, y próximos lanzamientos sin reseñas que quedan abajo en el ranking.
risks.mitigation: Se indexan los nombres en español, con alias, números romanos, búsqueda aproximada por trigramas y candidatos por inicio de título aunque no estén entre los más populares. Un conjunto de 300 consultas sirve de test de regresión, y más adelante se añadirán señales de IGDB.

risks.risk: La beta de Achievement Sets cambia lo que significa tener el 100% de los logros; además, muchos perfiles son privados.
risks.mitigation: Platinado siempre se marca a mano o se sugiere, nunca automáticamente. Los mensajes de privacidad explican qué ajuste cambiar.

risks.risk: Cumplir el ToU de Steam y el RGPD al añadir la sync y la integración con Steam (M4-M5).
risks.mitigation: Checklist obligatoria antes de lanzar: política de privacidad e información por capas, registro de actividades con Facilita RGPD, borrado y exportación, edad mínima de 14 años, aviso de marcas de Valve y ninguna analítica sin consentimiento.

result.why_this_wins:
- Velocidad sin red. Todo el catálogo (~196,6k juegos) vive en un SQLite FTS5 nativo; cada consulta mide 0,14-0,45 ms. No hay WASM, no hay índices de 11,5 MiB que descargar y el navegador no puede borrar el almacenamiento. El presupuesto de 50 ms va sobrado, con ~10-15 ms estimados de la tecla al pintado.
- Captura en escritorio sin rival para quien juega en PC. Atajo global con la ventana ya creada, detección del enlace en el portapapeles, bookmarklet, deep link y bandeja. Apuntar un juego mientras ves un tráiler o juegas en el mismo PC lleva 1,5-2 s, sin cambiar de ventana.
- El HTTP nativo elimina el problema de CORS. Las llamadas sin clave (portadas, nombres ES, wishlist, logros) salen del dispositivo sin proxy ni servidor: coste 0 € y la carga se reparte entre las IPs de los usuarios. La clave sigue en el CI y en el servidor, como exige el ToU.
- Offline y duradero desde el primer minuto. El seed viene en el instalador, los datos están en disco (sin el borrado a los 7 días de Safari) y hay backups automáticos.
- Usa lo que ya está instalado en esta máquina (Rust MSVC, Build Tools, WebView2, Node) y nada más: sin Docker, Postgres, Python ni pnpm.
- Infraestructura mínima y gratuita: ficheros estáticos en Cloudflare más un cron. El único servicio dinámico (Worker + D1) llega en M4/M5 y es opcional.
- Camino al móvil sin reescribir. La UI React y ga-core se reutilizan tal cual en Tauri Android, y la PWA cubre iOS y Android ya en M4.
- Calidad profesional con poco código. El núcleo Rust, separado de Tauri, se testea en el CI de Linux, y la búsqueda se valida contra un oráculo de fuerza bruta. Cada presupuesto se mide en el WebView2 real.
result.honest_weaknesses:
- Lo más habitual en una agenda es apuntar desde el móvil, y aquí no hay captura móvil hasta M4. iOS no tendrá nunca app nativa (no hay Mac), y en iOS la PWA no aparece en el menú de compartir (no hay Web Share Target).
- Hay más piezas que en una PWA pura: dos lenguajes, dos motores de búsqueda y de almacenamiento (FTS5 en escritorio, índice JS en la PWA) y lógica duplicada que hay que mantener alineada con tests compartidos.
- Distribuir cuesta más. Hay que bajar e instalar un instalador, y sin firma salen avisos de SmartScreen (la firma barata de Azure no parece accesible para particulares en la UE). Además hay claves del updater que custodiar y no existe un enlace web para probarla al momento.
- Las llamadas sin clave desde cada cliente dependen de endpoints no documentados. Valve puede cambiarlos o limitarlos, y sin telemetría es difícil diagnosticar fallos en los equipos de los usuarios.
- Windows primero: macOS y Linux no se prueban. Tauri los soporta, pero no hay Mac para probar ni firmar, y el E2E por CDP solo sirve para WebView2.
- Varias cifras son estimaciones que se medirán en M1 y M4: IPC, render, importación inicial (2-5 s), tamaño de catalog.db (~30-40 MiB) y rendimiento en móviles.
- El relay de sync propio (gana la última escritura por campo) es simple pero no está probado a fondo: si se edita la misma nota a la vez en dos sitios, se pierde una de las dos.
- Los próximos lanzamientos no tienen reseñas y salen abajo en el ranking por popularidad. Hace falta otra señal; podría venir de IGDB más adelante.
- Rust alarga los tiempos de compilación y la curva de aprendizaje para un desarrollador en solitario. Una sola persona tiene que mantener el núcleo Rust, la UI TS y el pipeline.

result.lens: Core use case and speed: capture a game in < 3 s from desktop AND phone, instant full-catalog search, offline behaviour, status/flag UX, perceived-performance budgets, and search-result quality (normalization, ranking, games-only).

criteria.criterion: Capture < 3 s on desktop AND phone
criteria.rationale: The phone side is strong. On Android, the installed PWA's share target auto-adds with undo (about 1.5 s), and the 'Apuntar juego' shortcut opens with search focused. The warm path (tap, 3-5 letters, tap) takes about 2 s. Burst capture and a long-press state picker are included. Title-only manual add and link paste work offline before the catalog exists. iOS only has the paste chip (about 3-4 s). Desktop has no OS-level hotkey, only in-app '/' and Ctrl+K plus the jump-list shortcut, so finding or launching the window uses up much of the budget. Sync is deferred to post-prototype M6, so phone and desktop captures end up in two separate agendas that can only be merged by manual export/import.

Search runs in a worker on a bitset word-prefix index (measured 0-0.3 ms). One-letter bitsets and early exit in static-rank order cap the worst case for 1-2 letter queries. There is no debounce, the latest seq wins, and at most 30 rows cross postMessage. Weak spots: the index is rebuilt on every cold start (estimated 1-1.5 s on phones), and the brute-force fallback during that time is 7-14 ms on this PC, plausibly 30-70 ms on a phone. A persisted index exists only as a fallback. On a first visit there is no catalog search until about 2.2 MB has been downloaded, parsed and indexed.

The base is sound: accent folding, apostrophes deleted (so 'baldurs' and 'garrys' work), an exact-title map, roman-numeral aliases, Spanish names indexed and shown, a compact-substring fallback, type 0 only, +18 hidden, a 'Retirado' badge, and a 100-query golden set (top-1 >= 90%). Defects: NFKD runs before ™ is removed. There are no acronym aliases. M1 has no popularity and no release state. Coming-soon games are penalized, although upcoming games are prime 'quiero jugar' captures. The 200-candidate cap can drop obscure title-start matches, and leading articles are not handled.

Offline is the normal state: precached shell, catalog in CacheStorage, IndexedDB writes, provisional entries from the URL slug, queued detail-shard fetches and runtime-cached covers. Durability depends only on storage.persist(), install prompts and manual export, and Safari deletes the storage of non-installed sites after 7 days. The first visit needs the network, which is unavoidable.

The model is right and ships in M2: 5 exclusive Estados and an open flag set (Platinado => Completado in one change set, Comprado, Próximo pinned). It also has a note, auto-stamped editable dates, a 5 s undo toast and tombstones. Results show 'Ya en tu agenda · Jugando' chips, a long-press picker sets the state at add, and every change is one tap from the agenda or from results. Two things are missing: keyboard shortcuts for states, and a rule for what happens to Platinado when the game is replayed.

The most rigorous of the three: every budget has both a mechanism and a gate. A Playwright project at CDP 4x asserts keystroke p95 <= 50 ms over about 600 keystrokes. Taps are measured with Event Timing, and a Lighthouse mobile gate is set at LCP 2.0 s. Other gates: JS <= 90 KB brotli, an offline second-launch scenario and a 20% regression gate. It also uses a reference Android and an in-app p50/p95 panel, which is the only way to measure an iPhone without a Mac.

factual_errors: fold() applies NFKD before removing ™. NFKD rewrites ™ as 'TM' (and ℠ as 'SM'), so the removal step never sees it: 'The Division™ 2' folds to 'the divisiontm 2', which breaks exact-title matches for the ~1k names with trademark symbols. B gets this order right.
The claim that compact() makes 'cs2' match is false. 'Counter-Strike 2' compacts to 'counterstrike2', which does not contain 'cs2'; acronyms need an alias list.

The M1 tie-break 'released before coming soon' does nothing. The M1 core carries only GetAppList fields (appid, name, last_modified, price_change_number), and its flag/year/pop columns stay zero until M2. M1 ranking is therefore effectively shortest-name-first, so short obscure titles outrank popular ones.

criteria.criterion: Capture < 3 s on desktop AND phone
criteria.rationale: Desktop capture is the best of the three: global Ctrl+Shift+Space (chosen to avoid AltGr), a pre-created hidden Quick-add window (<= 100 ms), clipboard Steam-link preselect, Enter / Shift+Enter bursts, Alt+1..5 for states, and a bookmarklet to the gameagenda:// deep link. That gives about 1.5-2 s from any app. But M1-M3 (about 18 dev-days) have no phone capture at all. M4 adds a separate React PWA: its share target needs an extra 'Añadir' tap, and iOS gets paste or a Shortcut to the inbox. Its captures reach the desktop only through a relay that is opt-in and off by default. The installer and the SmartScreen warning come before any first capture.

Native FTS5 trigram (measured 0.14-0.45 ms) uses rowid = popularity key, so ORDER BY rowid LIMIT returns the most popular matches first. A p1/p2 B-tree path handles 1-2 characters, and IPC adds 1-3 ms. The index lives on disk, so nothing is rebuilt at restart. The seed in the installer plus a brute-force bridge allow searching within about 3 s on a first run, even offline. The phone side (M4) is a JS prefix index that is not persisted.

The strongest design: ™ stripped before NFKD, ligatures, a leading-article-stripped key, title-start candidates injected, tiers for exact / title-start / word-prefix / substring, roman numerals 1-20, an alias CSV, trigram fuzzy matching, no penalty for coming-soon, and large golden sets. But its fold turns apostrophes into spaces. As a result 'baldurs gate', 'garrys mod', 'dont starve' and 'five nights at freddys' miss both the trigram MATCH and the title-prefix range until the M3 fuzzy stage. Its M1 tests (exact names, 4-letter prefixes) cannot catch this. Substring-first retrieval, capped at 400 by popularity, can push out word-prefix hits. The M4 PWA ranks with a different engine.

Desktop is best-in-class: the installer seed allows an offline first run, user.db uses WAL with synchronous=FULL, a daily VACUUM INTO backup runs, catalog.db can be regenerated, and there is no browser eviction. The phone only gets offline support in M4. That PWA has no source of cover URLs: the snapshot has no paths, browsers cannot call GetItems, and there is no proxy route.

It has A's model plus user-defined flags (flag_def), a 20-step undo stack with Ctrl+Z, keys 1-5 / P / C / N / Supr, Alt+1..5 at add, and editable auto-stamped dates, all in M2. That is the best desktop status UX; the phone gets it only in M4.

For the desktop it measures in the right places: Playwright over CDP on the real WebView2, a Rust search_bench (p95 <= 2 ms), Event Timing, web-vitals INP and a 10-launch startup script. Phone budgets are only measured from M4, and the CI thresholds are deliberately loose.

fatal_flaws: Fatal for this lens. Phone capture is missing for M1-M3 (about 18 dev-days), and the phone is the main capture device for a 'jot it down in seconds' agenda, so the core loop cannot be validated where it mostly happens. Even if M4 is pulled forward as B suggests, it arrives as a second stack (React PWA + JS prefix index + Dexie, with no covers) whose ranking and data differ from the Rust/FTS5 desktop. This is why B ranks below C despite the tied total.
factual_errors: fold() maps apostrophes to spaces ('Baldur's Gate 3' becomes 'baldur s gate 3'). Queries typed without the apostrophe ('baldurs gate', 'garrys mod', 'dont starve') therefore match neither the trigram MATCH nor the norm_na range, which contradicts its M1 search-quality claims for some of Steam's most popular titles.

pop = floor(2·log2(review_count+1)) is said to range 0-41, but it exceeds 41 above about 1.48M reviews. Counter-Strike 2 has several million reviews, giving about 45. It does no harm only because 63 − pop stays positive in k.

The stateless daily job finds 'cambios (last_modified distinto)' by comparing against the published snapshot. The published TSV has no last_modified column, so that change detection cannot work as specified.

criteria.criterion: Capture < 3 s on desktop AND phone
criteria.rationale: The PWA works on both devices from M1. It opens on Apuntar with a bottom bar within thumb reach, and one tap on a row adds the game. The field clears and keeps focus for bursts, and Android gives a haptic tap. The share target auto-adds, and Ctrl/Cmd+V anywhere parses links. Unknown or unlisted appids resolve in about 200-400 ms, and a first-time user can capture before the catalog is on the device. Guest sync (with pairing in M2) gives one agenda across devices. Desktop still has no OS-level shortcut, and iOS can only paste.

The typed-array prefix index is persisted in IndexedDB (restore in about 0.1-0.4 s), which gives the fastest cached restart of the web options. The first-visit fallback is server search (about 150-300 ms on 4G, debounced 120 ms): usable, but not instant, and Save-Data users stay on it permanently. There is no dedicated client path for 1-2 letter queries, which produce huge unions on phones. The catalog itself is served through the Worker, so it counts against the request quota. Common-token shards such as 'the' risk exceeding the 10 ms CPU cap.

It deletes apostrophes correctly, handles roman numerals, indexes Spanish names as aliases, adds CJK/Kana bigrams and scores every candidate. But it has the same NFKD-before-™ bug and no acronyms. It penalizes coming-soon games. Its popularity has only 16 levels and tops out at about 32k reviews, so blockbusters tie. Quality is checked by about 5 smoke queries; there is no golden set.

A local replica and outbox mean reads and taps never wait for the network, with a persisted index and a precached shell. Once data has synced, Safari's eviction loses nothing. But the server fills in covers on the next pull, so games added offline have no cover. The catalog and deltas come through the Worker, and a guest who loses the cookie before linking loses the list.

The model is correct: 5 Estados, Platinado forcing Completado with invariant repair at merge time, Comprado, Próximo, a note, auto-stamped dates and undo. But it only ships in M3, after accounts and pairing (M2), and every new flag needs a D1 migration.

Solid. Keystrokes and taps are tested at CDP 4x, and a long-task observer fails the E2E run. Lighthouse CI gates LCP at 2.0 s, cached restarts get timing marks, and a real Android device is used. Weaker points: the initial JS budget is 130 KB gzip, and the first-visit and Save-Data search paths are explicitly exempt from the 50 ms budget.

factual_errors: fold() also runs NFKD before dropping ™, so ™ survives as 'tm' attached to the preceding word.

The ~1-3 ms CPU claim for tier-2 search is unsupported for common tokens. Oversized shards are only split down to 3 characters, so a shard such as 'the' still holds tens of thousands of docs. Parsing it on a cold isolate can exceed the 10 ms Free CPU limit.

graft_ideas.idea: Fold order and ligatures: strip ™ ℠ ® © and every apostrophe form (' ’ ‘ ʼ) before NFKD, and map ß→ss, æ→ae, œ→oe, ø→o, ł→l, đ→d. Use one set of JSON test vectors for the worker, the pipeline and the tests. Delete apostrophes as A and C do; never turn them into spaces as B does.
graft_ideas.why: It removes the 'divisiontm' artefact in A and C without importing B's 'baldurs gate' miss.

graft_ideas.idea: Inject title-start candidates using an article-stripped key, and rank in tiers (exact > title-start > all tokens word-prefix > substring), using popularity only inside a tier. Never penalize coming-soon games.
graft_ideas.why: Obscure exact or prefix titles can no longer fall behind A's 200-candidate cutoff. Upcoming games have zero reviews but are prime 'quiero jugar' captures, and they stay visible.

graft_ideas.idea: Ship an alias CSV with the snapshot (gta, rdr2, cs2, ff7…), use roman numerals 1-20, and offer trigram/uFuzzy '¿Quizás buscabas…?' only when results are scarce.
graft_ideas.why: Players search by acronym, and A's compact() cannot produce acronyms.

graft_ideas.idea: The Quick-add pattern, as an optional thin Tauri 2 shell around the same web build once sync exists. It has a global hotkey that avoids Ctrl+Alt (AltGr on Spanish keyboards), a pre-created hidden always-on-top window, clipboard Steam-link preselect, Shift+Enter bursts and Alt+1..5 to set the state at add.
graft_ideas.why: It is the only way to capture in about 1.5-2 s from any Windows app. The prerequisites are already installed, and it needs no second search engine.

graft_ideas.idea: An iOS share-sheet Shortcut that POSTs the shared Steam URL to a write-only, revocable /inbox token.
graft_ideas.why: iOS has no Web Share Target. With this Shortcut a game is captured from the Steam app in about 2 s without opening Safari or the PWA.

graft_ideas.idea: Manual-then-match: a title captured before the catalog is ready is saved as a manual entry. It is linked to an appid automatically when exactly one catalog title matches after folding, and otherwise offered as a suggestion.
graft_ideas.why: Capture on a first visit or a slow network never waits for the ~2 MB download.

graft_ideas.idea: A pseudonymous pairing relay: a 256-bit secret is shared by QR code or URL fragment, and the server keeps only its hash. Changes are pushed and pulled through a D1 ops table, last write wins per field.
graft_ideas.why: It gives one agenda across phone and desktop inside the prototype, with no accounts or OpenID, and it plugs directly into A's HLC change log.

graft_ideas.idea: Quality gates at scale: 2,000 random exact names at >= 99% top-5, 4-letter prefixes of the 1,000 most popular games at >= 90% top-10, and 300 real Spanish queries including typos.
graft_ideas.why: A's 100-query set is too small to catch normalization regressions. Add cases typed without the apostrophe and acronym cases.

graft_ideas.idea: A keyboard-first agenda (1-5 for Estado, P/C/N for flags, Supr, Ctrl+Z with multi-step undo) plus user-defined flags (flag_def).
graft_ideas.why: It makes the desktop fast, and it covers the user's 'etc.' without migrations.

graft_ideas.idea: Persist the built typed-array index, keyed by catalog version, from M1 (restore in about 0.1-0.4 s).
graft_ideas.why: It removes the ~1-1.5 s rebuild on phones and A's over-budget brute-force window on every cold start.

graft_ideas.idea: Open on Apuntar with a bottom search bar within thumb reach. The whole row is the add button, the field clears and keeps focus, Android gives a 10 ms haptic tap, and Ctrl/Cmd+V anywhere parses Steam links.
graft_ideas.why: It saves a tap, supports one-handed bursts, and lets links be captured from any screen.

graft_ideas.idea: CJK/Hangul/Kana bigram tokens.
graft_ideas.why: They cover 6.3% of names, with better recall and speed than relying on the substring stage.

graft_ideas.idea: Pipeline publish gates that run smoke queries on the built index ('hollow knight' → 367520 at #1, 'baldurs gate' → 1086940 in the top 3, 'counter strike' → 730).
graft_ideas.why: A normalization or ranking regression never reaches clients.

graft_ideas.idea: A long-task observer that fails E2E on any main-thread task over 50 ms while typing or adding, plus single-tab sync with Web Locks, triggered on focus, online and visibility.
graft_ideas.why: It protects the keystroke and INP budgets, and background sync never blocks the UI.

graft_ideas.idea: Turn A's 'lazily loaded second file' into a popularity head file (about the top 20k games, ≈ 0.2-0.3 MB brotli) that is fetched first, with the tail fetched after load.
graft_ideas.why: First-visit search works in about 1 s on 4G from a static, offline-cacheable file. It replaces C's server search, which depends on the Worker and risks the CPU limit.

graft_ideas.idea: A bitset prefix index with ids in static-rank order, precomputed one-letter bitsets and early exit. It runs over a static, content-hashed catalog with deltas and details shards (fnv1a mod 1024) on Cloudflare static assets.
graft_ideas.why: It caps the 1-2 letter worst case on phones (C has no such path), keeps the hot path off any Worker quota, and gives a PWA a source for covers (B's companion has none).

graft_ideas.idea: A share target that auto-adds with undo, the 'Apuntar juego' manifest shortcut, provisional entries titled from the URL slug, and the in-app p50/p95 perf panel.
graft_ideas.why: Android capture takes one action (B needs an extra tap), link capture still works offline, and the panel is the only way to measure an iPhone without a Mac.

result.lens: Robustness, compliance and future-proofing: exposure to undocumented Steam endpoints and the fallbacks, key confidentiality and the Steam ToU, GDPR/LOPDGDD/LSSI, durability of user data (Safari eviction, backups, export, device loss), security and blast radius, the path to multi-device sync and multi-platform catalogs (IGDB, manual games, PlayStation), vendor lock-in.

criteria.criterion: Steam source robustness (undocumented endpoints, fallbacks, rate limits, catalog correctness)
criteria.rationale: The only hard dependency is the documented, keyed GetAppList (about 1 call/day plus 4/week). GetItems enrichment is a separate, schema-validated stage; if it fails, the snapshot still has names plus the last-known enrichment, and enrichmentAgeDays shows the age. Browsers never call Steam. Cover paths live in 1024 content-hashed static shards, so art keeps working through a GetItems outage. Gates are strong (at least 190k games, -2/+5% vs the last run, at most 1% name churn, sentinel appids, size cap). One worker runs at 0.4 req/s with a global 429 pause and checkpoints. Keyless Query covers the listing while the key is pending, and ES region-locked titles are re-queried with a US context. Minor gaps: reconcile is weekly, so removals can linger up to 7 days; enrichment rotates every 28 days; and the promised 24 h edge cache for appdetails is not assured on workers.dev (Cloudflare documents working Cache API operations for custom domains; C flags this).

Key handling is exemplary. The key lives only in GitHub and Worker secrets and travels only in the x-webapi-key header; CI greps the output for both the key and the header name; there are about 5 keyed calls/day, only to api.steampowered.com; the trademark notice is there and 'Steam' is not in the name or icon. But M5 Phase A exposes GET /api/v1/steam/library?steamid= with no authentication. Anyone can make our key fetch the library of any public profile. That breaks 'retrieve a user's data only as that user requests' and invites abuse that could get revoked the same key the catalog depends on. A postpones the fix (Sign in through Steam) to M6. CORS and a per-isolate token bucket are not access control.

Privacy by design. There is no server-side personal data before M5. The Worker is a no-store pass-through with logs off on /steam/*. No cookies and no analytics, so no banner is needed under LSSI 22.2. Import fields are minimised, export and delete exist, the Facilita RGPD record is planned before public release, images use referrerpolicy=no-referrer, and covers can be switched off. Gaps: the pasted-profile import runs other people's Steam data through our server, and the layered notice and aviso legal only arrive in M4, although hotlinked covers start sending IPs to Valve in M2.

criteria.criterion: User-data durability (Safari eviction, backups, export, device loss)
criteria.rationale: The stopgaps are good: persist() after the first add, install prompts against Safari's 7-day purge, full-fidelity JSON with HLC stamps plus CSV, idempotent import, a 30-day export reminder, and entries that carry their own title and cover. But for the whole prototype the only copy lives in one browser profile. A lost phone, a cleared browser or a deleted Home Screen app loses everything the user did not export by hand. Sync only comes after the prototype (M6).

The web hardening is solid: hash-mode CSP, nosniff and Permissions-Policy, text-only rendering, schema-validated imports capped at 10 MB and run in a worker, a fixed upstream allowlist, strict input validation, exact version pins, SHA-pinned actions and a key-leak grep. Weak points: (1) the unauthenticated keyed endpoint described above. (2) The pipeline's Cloudflare token ('Workers Scripts: Edit') covers the whole account. A compromised daily job, which ingests untrusted Steam data and runs third-party actions, could redeploy ga-web and read every user's local agenda. (3) /items and /details are unauthenticated relays to Steam from shared Cloudflare egress IPs, throttled only per isolate.

criteria.criterion: Future-proofing: multi-device sync, multi-platform catalogs, lock-in
criteria.rationale: Lock-in is the lowest of the three. The hot path is plain static files any host can serve, Hono is portable, and D1 only arrives for sync, with Turso/Neon as fallbacks. The catalog layer is source-agnostic, with an IGDB stage planned in the same job; flags are an open record; manual title-only games and platform chips exist from M1; the outbox and per-field HLC stamps exist from day one. But entry ids are random UUIDs with a separate unique gameKey. If two devices add the same Steam game offline, they create two entry streams, and the M6 server log (keyed by entry_id) has to collapse them. 'No redesign needed' is optimistic, and multi-device only arrives after the prototype.

fatal_flaws: M5 as written: GET /api/v1/steam/library?steamid= has no authentication, so the confidential key runs GetOwnedGames for any SteamID anyone submits. This breaks the ToU rule to retrieve a user's data only as that user requests, and it puts the key the catalog depends on at risk of abuse and revocation. Fatal for that milestone but cheap to fix: require Sign in through Steam (A's Phase B) before any per-user Steam call.

criteria.criterion: Steam source robustness (undocumented endpoints, fallbacks, rate limits, catalog correctness)
criteria.rationale: Diffing the full GetAppList every day (4 keyed calls) is a cheap daily reconcile. B also has a degraded mode (bit5), schema checks, a remote store_browse kill switch, and a full GetItems pass if Query breaks. But two undocumented endpoints sit in the core path: Query every week for popularity, adult flags and ES names, and GetItems for the rest. GetItems also runs in every client, because covers, ES names and dates are not in the snapshot. A Valve change therefore degrades every install, and the fix needs an updater release (the kill switch only stops the calls). The diff by last_modified cannot work from a published TSV that has no last_modified column. ES region-locked titles are never enriched.

The key lives only in GitHub and Worker secrets, never in the installer, binary or webview, and is sent only in the header. The keyed GetOwnedGames call happens only after a verified OpenID login, with a PKCE-style one-time handoff. There is a 'Datos de Steam que guardamos' screen, official buttons and a trademark notice. Minus: Level 1 lets anyone paste any profile and pull its wishlist and achievements. Those calls are keyless, but it is still someone else's data, fetched without their request. Also, the installer key-scan is placed in CI although the Windows builds are made on the dev PC.

Lean. The agenda stays on the device until M4. Sync spaces are pseudonymous: no email, and the server keeps only the sha256 of the secret. The steamID64 is never synced. There is a layered notice, a list of processors, Facilita, an age-14 checkbox and space deletion; the clipboard is read locally and never stored. Minus: GetOwnedGames results sit in D1 for 10 minutes, and the 'nothing is kept' claim ignores Time Travel, which is always on. The privacy notice is scheduled with M5, although covers and native Steam calls start in M2.

criteria.criterion: User-data durability (Safari eviction, backups, export, device loss)
criteria.rationale: The best local durability. user.db is SQLite (WAL, synchronous=FULL) outside any browser eviction, with daily VACUUM INTO backups (7 kept), copies before each migration, an optional copy to a user folder such as OneDrive, JSON export/import, and a separate, regenerable catalog.db. The M4 relay protects the PWA companion. Before M4, losing the PC is covered only if the user turned on the folder copy.

Tauri capabilities are locked down (no http, fs or shell in the webview), and network access goes only through Rust with allowlists. CSP is strict, SQL is parameterised with escaped MATCH tokens, untrusted responses have size and time caps, files are checked against the manifest's sha256, deep links have an action allowlist, the updater is signed with minisign, and pairing uses 256-bit secrets. Minus: a native app has a large blast radius, since a stolen updater key on a personal PC means code execution on every install. The installer is unsigned, which trains testers to click through SmartScreen. Manifest authenticity is left to the backlog, and the bearer space secret is embedded in an iOS Shortcut.

criteria.criterion: Future-proofing: multi-device sync, multi-platform catalogs, lock-in
criteria.rationale: Ids are natural keys (steam:, manual:, igdb:, psn:), a flag_def table allows custom flags, an HLC/LWW relay is designed, and the Rust core does not depend on Tauri, so Android can reuse it. But fold, link parsing, state rules and the LWW merge exist twice (Rust and TS) and must stay identical for sync to be correct, alongside two search and storage engines. The app is Windows-first on WebView2 and reaches mobile only at M4. Android needs the SDK, NDK, JDK and a Kotlin plugin; iOS only gets the PWA. IGDB needs a backend, which B lacks until M4. Tauri 3 churn is ahead.

factual_errors: Achievements at '2 llamadas por juego': the verified figure is about 1 call per game, so the estimate for the 500-game sweep (about 17 min) is inflated.

'Tras el traspaso, D1 no guarda ningún dato de Steam': D1 Time Travel is always on and allows point-in-time restores (7 days on Free), so the parked GetOwnedGames rows stay recoverable after the row is deleted. The transparency screen would understate retention.
The daily lane diffs 'last_modified distinto' with the published snapshot as its only state, but the published TSV has no last_modified column.

'Query no devuelve los títulos bloqueados en ES; esos se completan con GetItems': with country_code ES, GetItems answers those ids with success 15 + unvailable_for_country_restriction and no store data, so nothing gets completed. They can only be enriched from another country context.

criteria.criterion: Steam source robustness (undocumented endpoints, fallbacks, rate limits, catalog correctness)
criteria.rationale: The documented, keyed GetAppList is the only source for which games exist and their names. GetItems enrichment is additive, and the last good copy is kept. Zod contracts on every response, recorded fixtures and a nightly live canary give the best drift detection of the three. Smoke queries on the built index gate publishing; the manifest is written last; rollback exists; enrichment rotates every 7 days. R2 meta shards mean the API never needs Steam at request time, and Query is only a fallback. Minus: C runs at 1 req/s, 2.5 times the community-observed ~120 per 5 min, so 429 pauses from runner IPs are predictable. Catalog downloads go through the Worker (/catalog/*), sharing the 100k/day quota with sync and auth. And the claim that dispatch is safe from the 60-day rule does not hold (see errors).

The best alignment of the three. The key lives only in GitHub and Worker secrets and is sent in the header, with at most 5 keyed calls/day. Imports happen only after Sign in through Steam and only on a tap; pasted-profile imports are explicitly refused because the profile could belong to someone else. The policy names which Steam data is stored and where (EU). Valve's official sign-in images and a trademark footer are used, and 'Steam' stays out of the name and icon.

The most complete paperwork: Art. 6(1)(b), no email, IP or password columns, pseudonymous guests, D1 and R2 in the EU jurisdiction, DPA/SCCs, a retention schedule (sessions 90 days, tombstones 90 days, inactive guests 13 months, Time Travel 7 days, disclosed), export and delete, Facilita, minimum age 14. But it creates server-side personal data (the library plus free-text notes) from the first add in M1, while privacy notice v1 only lands in M2 and the record of processing in M6. A sync cookie created silently is 'strictly necessary' under LSSI 22.2 only if sync is clearly presented as the service the user asked for.

criteria.criterion: User-data durability (Safari eviction, backups, export, device loss)
criteria.rationale: The server is authoritative from the first add. The device credential is a cookie set by the server as HttpOnly, and the M1 acceptance test proves 'delete IndexedDB, reload, library restored'. So Safari's purge, a cleared IndexedDB, or a lost phone (once linked or paired) cost only the ops not yet synced. Export to JSON/CSV works offline and through the API, and Time Travel comes with a restore drill. Minus: an unlinked guest who loses the cookie loses access. Time Travel (7 days, same vendor) is the only server backup. And last-writer-wins on the same field silently drops one of two concurrent edits.

The most rigorous auth: a __Host- cookie that is HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite=Lax; 256-bit tokens stored as hashes and rotated; Origin checks, body caps and Zod on every input; a cap on future HLC skew; OpenID with the ticket bound into the signed return_to plus a PKCE-style redeem; an HMAC-signed pipeline report; an R2 token scoped to the bucket and a separate deploy token. Minus: pairing codes have only 6 digits (a million values), and the only real guard is a best-effort limiter per Cloudflare location. An attacker can enumerate codes within the free quota and pair into a victim's account, and the same flood takes sync and catalog downloads down. It also has the largest attack surface of the three (guest creation, account merges, and a dev-only R2 upload route that must never ship).

criteria.criterion: Future-proofing: multi-device sync, multi-platform catalogs, lock-in
criteria.rationale: Sync and multi-device work from M1, with deterministic ids and one merge() shared by client and server, including invariant repair, property tests and e2e tests with two browser contexts. A backend already exists for IGDB (which is backend-only), Steam import and future reminders; manual games and igdb: ids are planned. Minus: flags are columns, so every new flag is a migration. Cloudflare coupling is the deepest of the three: D1's SQL dialect, R2 jurisdiction, Cron Triggers, the Rate Limiting binding, Time Travel and catalog delivery through the Worker. It is portable in principle (Hono on Node, Drizzle to libSQL/node:sqlite, plain files), but moving would be a real port.

factual_errors: 'Dispatch is not affected by the rule that disables scheduled workflows after 60 days': in a public repo, GitHub auto-disables the workflow itself, and catalog.yml also carries the backup schedule. GitHub says disabling stops a workflow 'from being triggered', which includes dispatch, until it is re-enabled. The fix is a private repo, the schedule in a separate file, or an enable-workflow call before dispatching.

'The D1 attempt counter is the strict guard' for 6-digit pairing codes: a counter kept per code never sees guesses that match no code, so it gives no brute-force protection. Only the best-effort per-location limiter does.

graft_ideas.idea: Clients never call Steam APIs. The pipeline bakes cover paths (library_capsule, then header, then none), release dates and review data into 1024 static shards, hashed with fnv1a and named by content hash; unchanged shards keep their hash.
graft_ideas.why: A GetItems break only freezes enrichment on the server: no client release is needed, users' IPs never reach api.steampowered.com, and covers keep working.

graft_ideas.idea: Keep the app shell and the catalog on Workers Static Assets, and use the Worker only for optional /api routes.
graft_ideas.why: Static requests are unlimited and do not count against the 100k/day Worker quota. Running out of quota, a Worker bug or a move off Cloudflare can never break search or capture.

graft_ideas.idea: Publish gates: at least 190k games, -2%/+5% against the previous run, at most 1% of names changed, sentinel appids, strict parsing, a size cap. Add enrichmentAgeDays to the manifest, skip publishing and open an issue automatically on failure, and emit byte-identical output for identical input.
graft_ideas.why: The catalog cannot regress silently, and clients can see how stale it is.

graft_ideas.idea: CI fails if any build output contains the key value or the string 'x-webapi-key'.
graft_ideas.why: Key confidentiality becomes an enforced check rather than a policy.

graft_ideas.idea: Keep a per-field HLC change log and a full-fidelity export that includes the stamps, so that import runs through the same LWW merge as sync. Store flags as an open record.
graft_ideas.why: Import, restore and sync share one merge path, and new 'etc.' flags need no migration.

graft_ideas.idea: Use natural primary keys (steam:<appid>, manual:<uuidv7>, igdb:<id>) instead of a random UUID plus a unique gameKey.
graft_ideas.why: If two devices add the same game offline, both end up with one row instead of two entry streams.

graft_ideas.idea: Fetch the full GetAppList every day (4 keyed calls) and diff it against stored pipeline state that keeps last_modified for each appid.
graft_ideas.why: Removals and delistings show up within 24 h and cursor bugs fix themselves, for about 5 keyed calls/day against the 100k cap.

graft_ideas.idea: Treat the manifest as a control plane: remote kill switches (store_browse:false, a minimum client version) and an ed25519 signature checked against a public key built into the app.
graft_ideas.why: It gives an emergency brake for Steam-dependent features. A sha256 inside the same manifest only proves integrity; the signature proves authenticity even if the CDN or the deploy token is compromised.

graft_ideas.idea: A 'Datos de Steam que guardamos' screen that lists each piece of Steam data, where it lives (the device, Cloudflare in the EU, Valve in the USA via the image CDN), and one delete button.
graft_ideas.why: It puts the ToU duty to tell users which Steam data is stored, and in which countries, into the UI.

graft_ideas.idea: Pair devices with a single-use, high-entropy secret (128 bits or more) carried in a QR code or URL fragment; the server stores only its hash.
graft_ideas.why: Multi-device without email and without 6-digit codes that can be brute-forced.

graft_ideas.idea: Make no per-user Steam call, keyed or keyless, before a verified Sign in through Steam, and refuse pasted-profile imports. Bind the ticket into the signed return_to and redeem it with a PKCE-style verifier.
graft_ideas.why: It meets 'retrieve a user's data only as that user requests', blocks login and account-linking CSRF, and works with the separate cookie jar of iOS Home Screen apps.

graft_ideas.idea: Zod contracts on every Steam response, recorded fixtures in CI, a nightly live canary, and smoke queries on the built index as a publish gate.
graft_ideas.why: It catches changes in the undocumented endpoints before users see them, and checks that search works, not just that counts match.

graft_ideas.idea: Use a __Host- session cookie, set by the server as HttpOnly and holding a hashed 256-bit token, as the device credential. Make 'wipe IndexedDB, reload, library restored' an acceptance test on a real iPhone.
graft_ideas.why: WebKit's 7-day rule targets storage that scripts can write; a secret held in JavaScript would disappear along with IndexedDB.

graft_ideas.idea: Create D1 and R2 in the EU jurisdiction, write a retention schedule that includes Time Travel (always on, 7 days on Free), and run restore and catalog-rollback drills.
graft_ideas.why: It covers storage limitation and transparency, and tests recovery instead of assuming it.

graft_ideas.idea: Least-privilege publishing: the pipeline holds only a credential scoped to the R2 bucket or to a separate account, never one that can redeploy the app.
graft_ideas.why: A compromised daily job that ingests untrusted Steam data can at worst poison catalog data; it cannot ship code.

graft_ideas.idea: A Cloudflare Cron Trigger dispatches the pipeline, and an hourly watchdog dispatches it again when the manifest is older than 30 h. Extend it to call GitHub's enable-workflow endpoint first.
graft_ideas.why: Catalog freshness stops depending on GitHub's best-effort schedule and its 60-day auto-disable.

graft_ideas.idea: One merge() with invariant repair (the newer clock decides Platinado versus Completado), shared clocks for status and its dates, property tests and Playwright tests with two browser contexts.
graft_ideas.why: Sync correctness is proven, not assumed.

result.recommended_synthesis:
A ranks last as written only because of two sequencing faults: the keyed Steam import is unauthenticated, and there is no server copy of user data during the prototype. Its hot path and catalog are still the soundest base. The synthesis keeps them, adds C's durability and identity layer, and takes B's ids and manifest control plane. Hot path and catalog: A's static, installable PWA, with a prefix index in a Web Worker and optimistic writes to IndexedDB. No browser ever calls a Steam API, and the Worker is never involved in search or capture. The pipeline runs on Node 24 in a private GitHub repo. Its one hard dependency is the documented IStoreService/GetAppList/v1, with the key sent only in the x-webapi-key header from a GitHub secret. It fetches the full list daily (4 calls, as in B) and diffs it against stored state (appid, name, last_modified, price_change_number). Removals and delistings then show up within 24 h, for about 5 keyed calls/day; if_modified_since remains an optimisation. New and changed ids, plus a rotating 1/14 slice of the catalog, are enriched through keyless GetItems: country_code ES, language spanish, include_best_purchase_option=false, at most 200 ids per GET, one worker at 0.4 req/s, exponential backoff and a global pause on 429. Ids that vanish are classified: unlisted:true becomes 'Retirado', appid 0 is removed, region-locked titles stay flagged and are enriched from a US context. Every Steam response is checked against Zod contracts, with recorded fixtures in CI and a nightly live canary (from C). Publish gates combine A's checks (counts, sentinel appids, name churn, size) with C's smoke queries on the built index. If enrichment fails, the names still publish with the last-known enrichment and a growing enrichmentAgeDays. The output is A's core TSV, deltas and 1024 content-hashed details shards with cover paths: library_capsule, then header, then no cover, never a guessed filename. The manifest is signed with ed25519 and carries remote kill switches (from B). Everything is served from Workers Static Assets, deployed from a separate Cloudflare account, so the pipeline's credential cannot redeploy the app. For freshness, the GitHub schedule is backed by a Cloudflare Cron watchdog. When the manifest is older than 30 h, it re-enables the workflow and dispatches it; dispatch inputs are never interpolated into shell commands. Unknown or delisted appids that users paste are resolved on demand through the Worker: GetItems also answers for unlisted games, and appdetails is used only for the Ficha. Fallbacks are the keyless IStoreQueryService/Query listing if the key is missing or revoked, and the jsnli dump as a dev fixture only.

User data lives in Dexie with natural ids: steam:<appid>, manual:<uuidv7>, later igdb:<id>. Each entry has one of the five exclusive Estados, an open flags record (Platinado also sets Completado; Comprado, Próximo and custom flags), its own copy of title and cover, and per-field HLC stamps written to an outbox from the first commit. On top of that come storage.persist(), install prompts, A's full-fidelity JSON export with stamps plus CSV, import through the same LWW merge, and an automatic local snapshot before every schema migration or bulk import. The cloud copy moves from post-prototype to the milestone right after Estados and flags. It is an explicit one-tap 'Guardar copia y sincronizar', offered after the first few adds and whenever iOS Safari is used without installing. Because the user asks for it, its cookie counts as strictly necessary under LSSI 22.2, and no agenda data reaches our server before that. The protocol is C's: one POST /api/v1/sync per round trip, a per-user sequence number on the server, and one merge() shared by client and server with invariant repair and shared clocks. It is covered by property tests and Playwright tests with two browser contexts, and runs on a Hono Worker with D1 in the EU jurisdiction. The device credential is a __Host- cookie set by the server as HttpOnly, holding a hashed 256-bit token (from C). WebKit's 7-day rule targets storage that scripts can write, so a secret held in JavaScript, as in B, would disappear with IndexedDB. Prove the cookie approach on a real iPhone: wipe IndexedDB, reload, and check the library is restored. Pairing a new device uses a single-use token of at least 128 bits in a QR code or URL fragment, confirmed on the originating device: B's entropy, not C's 6-digit codes. Sign in through Steam is the optional way to recover an account. D1 is backed up beyond Time Travel with a weekly export into an EU R2 bucket. The export runs inside Cloudflare, and its short retention is disclosed.

Steam account and compliance. No per-user Steam call, keyed or keyless, happens before a verified Sign in through Steam. This is C's flow: OpenID 2.0, server-side check_authentication with steam-signin 1.0.5, the ticket bound into the signed return_to, and a PKCE-style redeem that works with the separate cookie jar of iOS Home Screen apps. After sign-in the Worker calls:
- GetOwnedGames with the key, to set Comprado. Family-shared games are excluded, playtime is only a hint, and the app shows Spanish guidance when 'Detalles de juego' is private.
- The keyless wishlist.
- Per-game achievements, which only suggest Platinado because the Achievement Sets beta changes what 100% means.
Results come back in the response and are never stored in D1. /steam/* responses are no-store, with logging off. Legal texts ship together with the data they cover:
- The first-layer notice ships with the first milestone that hotlinks covers, which sends IPs to Valve; images use referrerpolicy=no-referrer and a 'Cargar portadas' switch turns them off.
- The full policy, the aviso legal and the Facilita RGPD record are in place before the first outside tester and before sync.
- B's 'Datos de Steam que guardamos' screen and C's retention schedule (sessions, tombstones, inactive accounts, Time Travel, backups).
- Turning on sync asks for a declaration of age 14 or older, ready to change to 16.
- No analytics without consent, a trademark notice, Valve's official sign-in images, and 'Steam' kept out of the name and icon.

Security and future-proofing. Keep A's hash-mode CSP and security headers, text-only rendering and schema-validated imports. The Worker gets a fixed upstream allowlist, Zod on every input, Origin checks on non-GET requests, body caps, and rate limits on every unauthenticated route (session creation, pairing, resolve). The free 100k/day quota is itself a denial-of-service surface, one more reason to keep the hot path static. Keep CI's key-leak grep, exact version pins, SHA-pinned actions and narrowly scoped tokens. Get a custom domain before relying on the Cache API. Lock-in stays low: the hot path is plain files any static host can serve, Hono runs on Node, and the SQL stays portable to libSQL/Turso or node:sqlite. For other platforms, IGDB arrives as a pipeline stage: backend-only, 4 req/s, with visible attribution. It maps Steam titles through external_games source 1, so they keep steam:<appid> and only non-Steam titles get igdb:<id>. Manual entries carry an optional catalogRef, so they can be linked to a catalog game later without changing their id. PlayStation 'platinado' stays manual (no NPSSO). Tauri on desktop (global shortcut) and Capacitor remain optional wrappers over the same PWA. B's Rust core is not adopted, so text folding, ranking and merge exist in exactly one TypeScript implementation.

result.lens: Feasibility for ONE developer on THIS machine (Windows 11, Node 24.21/npm 11.19, Rust 1.99, no Docker/Postgres/Mac): time to first useful prototype, moving parts, learning curve, running cost and free-tier traps, maintainability, testing/CI simplicity. On 2026-10-28 I spot-checked the version and limit claims against the npm registry, crates.io, the steam-signin 1.0.5 source and the current Cloudflare/GitHub docs.

criteria.rationale: No server code until M4. After M0+M1 (7.5 planned days) the PWA searches all ~196.6k games and saves to 'Quiero jugar' on Android and desktop, and manual/link add work before the catalog loads. But M1 also carries the whole cron pipeline (backfill, delta, reconcile, gates, Release state) next to search, Explorar and offline, so 6 days is roughly 2x optimistic, and estados/flags wait for M2.

One language. For the prototype it is just static files plus one Actions job. graft_ideas.idea: Make the pipeline a single daily mode: the full GetAppList (4 keyed calls) diffed against stored state. Keep last_modified in that state, which fixes B's gap.
graft_ideas.why: It replaces A's if_modified_since cursor and the separate weekly reconcile. Deletions are caught every day, every run is idempotent, and 4 calls/day is nothing against the 100k/day cap.

graft_ideas.idea: Ping a dead-man switch (e.g. healthchecks.io) after each successful pipeline run, and show the catalog's age in Ajustes.
graft_ideas.why: GitHub emails when a run fails, but not when a schedule is delayed, dropped under load (documented) or never fires.

graft_ideas.idea: Put remote kill-switch flags in manifest.json, for example to turn off features that depend on GetItems or to stop loading covers.
graft_ideas.why: Lets one person react to a change in an undocumented Steam endpoint without shipping a new client.

graft_ideas.idea: Use natural primary keys 'steam:<appid>' or 'manual:<uuidv7>' instead of a random UUID plus a unique gameKey (C does the same).

result.recommended_synthesis:
I would ship A, trimmed to what one person can finish in about three weeks on this PC, plus the best operational ideas from B and C. It is one TypeScript repo on npm workspaces, which are already installed (with .npmrc save-exact, .gitattributes eol=lf and core.longpaths):
- apps/web: a React 19.3.1 + Vite 8.3.5 SPA with a hand-written static shell in index.html for LCP. It uses @vitejs/plugin-react 6.1.2, @tanstack/react-virtual 3.14.23 for Explorar, vite-plugin-pwa 2.0.0 (injectManifest) and Dexie 4.4.7.
- packages/core: fold/tokenize, A's word-prefix index with substring fallback and roman-numeral aliases, ranking, the Steam-link parser, the TSV/shard codecs and the estado/flag rules, tested with Vitest 5.0.5 and a 100-query golden set.
- pipeline/: zero-dependency Node 24 .ts scripts run by type stripping.

TypeScript 7.0.2 (npm latest) is fine because nothing in this stack needs the compiler API; fall back to 6.0.3 only if some tool does. Lint with Biome 2.6.3, E2E with Playwright 1.64.1. I drop SvelteKit 3.1 even though A got it right (its Kit 3 details match the 3.1.0 package): a five-screen SPA needs no meta-framework, and Kit 3's moved config and service-worker modules make most tutorials and AI answers stale. The prototype has no server code, no database and no accounts. Two assets-only Workers on workers.dev serve it: ga-web deploys on every push and ga-catalog deploys data daily, and their static requests are free and unlimited. Never enable the new Workers Cache on them, because it bills static-asset requests that are otherwise free.

The catalog comes from one pipeline mode that runs the same way on the PC (node --env-file=.env pipeline/run.ts) and in a private-repo Actions cron at minute 17, plus workflow_dispatch. Each run:
1. Fetches the full IStoreService/GetAppList: 4 keyed calls, key only in x-webapi-key.
2. Diffs it against the master.ndjson.gz state (which includes last_modified), stored as a GitHub Release asset.
3. Calls keyless GetItems (country ES, language spanish, at most 200 ids per call, include_best_purchase_option=false, one worker at 0.4 req/s or less, global pause on 429) for added, changed and vanished ids plus a rotating 1/28 slice: about 52 calls/day.
4. Classifies: only type 0 enters; unlisted becomes 'Retirado'; success 15 with appid 0 is dropped; region-locked titles are kept.
5. Emits the core TSV (appid delta, name, flags, year, pop, esName) as text/plain, plus 1024 content-hashed detail shards. Each shard row carries the name, the cover/header path built from asset_url_format (library_capsule, then header, never guessed), the release date and reviews. Check in M0 that Cloudflare really compresses the core on the fly.
6. Runs the gates (count band, sentinel appids, smoke queries), deploys with wrangler, saves state and pings the dead-man switch.

Before the Steam key arrives, the M1 snapshot is built on the PC from the jsnli dump (prototype seed only), enriched by keyless GetItems (~983 calls, ~41 min). IStoreQueryService/Query (~197 calls) is the keyless fallback for the game list. Clients check the manifest every 12 h but re-download the ~2 MB core at most weekly or on demand. A pasted appid that is missing locally resolves from today's shard, so the prototype needs neither an /items endpoint nor a delta chain.

On the client, the Search Worker answers on every keystroke (0-0.3 ms measured on this PC) and uses a brute-force scan until the index is built; manual add and link paste work before the catalog loads. Entries are keyed 'steam:<appid>' or 'manual:<uuidv7>'. Each one carries one of the five estados, an open flag set (Platinado implies Completado; Comprado; Próximo), auto-stamped dates and per-field updatedAt stamps. There is no change log until sync; undo is an in-memory toast. Capture options:
- '+' or Enter, with a long-press picker for other states
- paste a link, the Android share target and manifest shortcuts
- '/' and Ctrl+K on desktop (no Ctrl+Alt combinations, because that is AltGr on Spanish keyboards)

Also included: navigator.storage.persist(), JSON export/import, adult titles hidden by default, the Valve trademark notice, and a covers switch next to the disclosure that covers are hotlinked from Valve.

Milestones:
- M0, 1-2 days: repo, CI, deploys, and the Steam key request.
- M1, 6-8 days: search, capture and the full estados/flags on the PC-built snapshot, usable on phone and desktop.
- M2, 3-4 days: cron automation, enrichment, covers and gates.
- M3, 3 days: PWA hardening.
- M4, optional: Steam import through one thin Hono 4.13 Worker (key as a secret, pass-through, no storage), tested with app.request() on Vitest 5.

After the prototype comes D1 sync in the EU jurisdiction, using steam-signin under nodejs_compat plus C's ticket redeem, tested through a cloudflared tunnel. Only then an optional Tauri 2 hotkey shell.

CI runs on ubuntu in 5 minutes or less per push: Biome, tsc, Vitest, Playwright Chromium E2E (add, offline, the /share route), size gates and the key-leak grep. Perf budgets run at 4x CDP throttling and are reported in CI, not gated. The hard gate is a local npm run perf plus a reference Android phone through chrome://inspect; the iPhone is checked through an HTTPS tunnel and an in-app perf panel. Running cost is €0/month: about 120-150 pipeline minutes plus CI fit inside the private repo's 2,000, and there is no D1 or R2 until sync. Remaining traps:
- Late or dropped schedules: a dead-man ping now, and C's Cloudflare-cron dispatch of a workflow without its own schedule if it becomes a problem.
- Shared GitHub runner IPs drawing 429s: run backfills from the PC.
- The Steam key prerequisites (at least US$5 spent and Steam Guard Mobile Authenticator): request the key on day 1.
